speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This Bill comes before Parliament in the midst of very serious challenges faced by us, which both Ministers and Members of Parliament have spoken about a number of times.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In my speech, I will explain why we need this intervention, explain the principles behind the Bill and set out the key features of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Just under two months ago, I moved an urgent Bill in this House – the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) Bill, which I will refer to as “COVID 1”.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: COVID 1 was, in itself, a major intervention.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In my speech then, I explained why intervention was needed – economic shock, unprecedented in magnitude in terms of impact and the speed with which the impact was felt.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I also set out the principles for such intervention.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The starting point is always the sanctity of contract – a fundamental, key aspect of the rule of law and we do not lightly intervene.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But sanctity of contract cannot be an absolute.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I said that intervention is needed when the core interests of our people are at stake and there is a need to safeguard the fundamental integrity of the economic structure for the common good.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Such intervention has to be reasonable and of generally limited duration.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In COVID 1, we put in what I called a “legal circuit breaker”.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It provided a framework to hold in abeyance the strict enforcement of certain legal rights for a period of time.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The objective was to give businesses some cash flow relief and breathing space to make adjustments.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, if a business tenant is unable to pay rent during the relief period because of COVID-19, the landlord cannot evict the tenant during the relief period.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At the time, I emphasised that COVID 1 only deferred contractual obligations.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I also explained to this House that the Bill gave businesses breathing space.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It also gave the Government some time to take in feedback, assess the evolving situation, conduct a deeper analysis and decide whether more substantive interventions were needed.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Over the past two months, we have done precisely that.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For many, including the businesses most affected by those measures, April now feels like a lifetime away.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Globally, we were looking at 1.2 million infections and 67, 000 dead.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As of 1 June, we are looking at more than 6 million infections and more than 370,000 dead.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Various restrictions had already been put in place by then, but the circuit breaker caused a substantial increase in the restrictions.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister and other Ministers have explained in considerable detail.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The economic situation and outlook has deteriorated substantially.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We are taking a cautious approach in lifting the circuit breaker measures.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And for some, the impact has been near catastrophic.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Latest data from the Department of Statistics, some just released today.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you look at F&B sales in March 2020, they declined by 23.7%.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Retail sales, if you exclude supermarkets, hypermarkets and convenience stalls, retail sales in March 2020 declined by 13.3%.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These numbers do not even show the full impact of the circuit breaker because data for May 2020 is not out yet.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We can, obviously, expect the numbers to be very weak.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Revenue has fallen but meanwhile fixed costs continue.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For many businesses, in the F&B, retail sector, two significant components of such costs are manpower and rent.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many landlords have taken a helpful approach and a long-term view.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They have shared the burden with their tenants.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Nevertheless , we received a lot of feedback from struggling SMEs that they need more time to recover.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many cannot operate until Phase Two, and even then only partially.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many landlords have rendered substantive assistance, but several others have not.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The point is that accumulated arrears should be handled fairly.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will share one piece of feedback as an illustration.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is a tenant who is a mother of two young children.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: She started a company two years ago, providing enrichment lessons to children.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: She leased some space for the business as a sub-tenant.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: She renewed her lease for one year, just before COVID-19 hit.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: All revenue that came in went to support the business – payment of rent, salaries for trainers and other operational costs.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But from February 2020, parents began to keep students away.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Her landlord has offered her 10% discount for April and May 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: COVID-19 is quite an unforeseeable event, both in magnitude and speed of impact.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is wiping out the hard work that many people have put in into their businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, if landlords insist on payments that tenants cannot afford, tenants will have to give up.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Landlords then have to take their chances to recover something in the insolvency proceedings, together with other creditors.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Landlords will then also have to find replacement tenants.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Therefore, it is in everyone’s interests to take a sensible approach, ensure everyone comes out of this together, ready to recover.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: After watching all of this carefully, taking in the feedback, looking at the numbers that were coming in, we decided that there is a need for a substantive intervention.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The challenge that rent poses to small businesses, is not a problem unique to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A number of other countries have seen that and they have intervened.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will just give the examples of Australia and Germany.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In Australia, landlords are required to offer rent waivers and deferrals to SME tenants.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And SME tenants are allowed to repay the deferred rent over a period of at least 24 months, interest-free.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In Germany, landlords are not allowed to terminate a tenancy for non-payment of rent.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And arrears with accumulated interest can be repaid before 30 June 2022; that means, two years of extension.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What is necessary in this situation is a fair sharing of obligations because of the exceptional times that are before us.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The fair sharing has got to be between the Government, the landlords and the tenants.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, if you look at the rest of the burden, what is a fair sharing of the remainder between landlords and tenants?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the related question is, will the market left to itself be able to find an equilibrium that reflects the principle of fairness?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The answer to these two related questions depends on a number of points.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, all Singaporeans, including landlords, have a shared interest in seeing our SMEs do well.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, in a climate like this, expecting market forces to push towards a fair equilibrium is not realistic.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Third, what is the alternative if we do not intervene?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: SMEs play, as I have said, a critical role in the Singapore economy.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If many of our SMEs for whom a stable cash flow is fundamental, are unable to survive, the domino effect on the rest of the economy will be very substantial and a lot of jobs will be at stake.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For landlords, their asset value will be affected by the broader economy.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There is a clear correlation between growth of property prices and economic growth.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If our SMEs do well, the economy is given a boost, property owners will continue to enjoy the stable value of their assets.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If viable SMEs go under because of temporary cash flow difficulties, the economy as a whole suffers, the value of property will also suffer.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, the essential point: everyone has a stake in the viability of the SMEs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, landlords will be required to ensure that the benefits of Governments assistance are given to the actual, intended beneficiaries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is, the SME tenants operating in rented premises and this will include licencees.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And third, SMEs who qualify for the rental waiver will also be given time to repay some of their remaining rental arrears, at an interest rate that will be capped.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As said earlier, most of these reliefs apply to SME tenants, including sub-tenants and licencees.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The rental relief framework will also apply to eligible Non-Profit Organisations and eligible tenants of Government properties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Deputy Prime Minister announced property tax rebates from the Resilience and Unity Budgets.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This will be done via rental waivers, granted by landlords.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Agencies are working out the details, which will give landlords clarity on the relief that they are required to offer; and give tenants clarity on the relief that they will get.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This will be set out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This will be calculated at the rental unit or outlet level.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Tenants must have entered into their tenancy before 25 March 2020, or extended such a tenancy to get this relief.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are smaller landlords who face genuine hardship.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, retirees who have purchased a small commercial property, and the rental yield from that property forms a very large proportion of their income.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For this group, they may seek an assessment on grounds of financial hardship.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The assessment will take into consideration the annual value of the landlord’s properties, and whether the rental income forms a substantial part of his or her total income.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Qualifying landlords will only be required to give half of the additional rental waivers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we will set out the criteria for landlords to qualify for this in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: During our consultations, stakeholders have asked for clarity on a few matters.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Landlords wanted more clarity on when their obligations will be triggered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Tenants wanted clarity on when they will be entitled to the relief.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For the landlords, their obligations will be triggered when IRAS issues the notice of the cash grant or nominal notice to eligible property owners.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: IRAS will provide more details of the cash grant on its website, once it works the details out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Meanwhile, to preserve the status quo, the Bill provides for a moratorium on enforcement action for non-payment of rent in the time between the Act coming into force and the triggering of the landlords’ obligations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even before the Act comes into force, tenants who are unable to pay their rent and require protection from eviction can serve a Notification for Relief under COVID 1, as it exists today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, we recognise that many landlords may have already given relief.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This could be in the form of rental waivers or rebates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These landlords will be able to set off the equivalent value against the amount of waiver that they are required to give under the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The kinds of reliefs that landlords have given and which can be taken into account for this purpose will be set out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Third, what if the tenant has already paid the rent for the months in which relief is meant to be granted or for the months for which relief is meant to be granted?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In such a situation, the landlord will be required to credit any amounts already paid to the tenant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This may be in the form of the waiver being applied in the next month of rent that is due.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the lease is coming to an end, the landlord will have to provide a refund to the eligible tenant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fourth, MAS has separately announced some additional relief from banks and finance companies in relation to landlords’ existing loan repayment obligations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Individual landlords who have been required to provide relief to their tenants under this Bill can apply to defer both principal and interest payments on their commercial and industrial property loans till the end of the year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, if moratorium is given until October for tenants; landlords will get assistance from their financial institutions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They can also apply for an extension of loan tenure by up to the corresponding deferment period to make the monthly instalments more manageable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: SME landlords who face financial difficulties can already apply to defer the principal repayments on their mortgages under the industry relief package that MAS announced some weeks ago.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Larger landlords can likewise work with their banks and finance companies if they require assistance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those who need to access additional credit to meet their immediate cashflow needs can either apply for mortgage equity withdrawal loans or loans under ESG’s Temporary Bridging Loan Programme or Working Capital Loan Scheme, if they qualify.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will have to start repaying the arrears from November 2020.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These arrears, of course, do not include, for example, the four months which have been waived – these are no longer payable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the tenancy is shorter, then, it has got to be paid during the term of the tenancy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For industrial and office properties, the maximum amount of arrears that can be paid in instalments will be four months’ base rent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This means that landlords take on some credit risk.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As a safeguard, we will provide that all outstanding arrears, including interest and other charges, will be accelerated and immediately payable in accordance with the terms of the original contract, if instalment payments under the scheme are not paid within the prescribed time after they become due; or if the tenant terminates or repudiates his lease agreement during the rescheduled repayment period; or if the lease agreement is terminated due to other defaults by the tenant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Landlords may also draw the existing security deposits to offset accumulated rental arrears during the repayment period.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They may do so, until there is the equivalent of at least one month of rent remaining in the security deposit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At the end of the repayment period, the tenant will be obliged to reinstate the security deposit, as provided in the contract.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In addition, we will require tenant who have rescheduled the payment of arrears, to provide specified documents and information to their landlords if the lease agreement is: one, terminated or repudiated during the repayment period; and two, there are two or more rescheduled repayment instalments outstanding.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The documents and information to be provided will include filing a statutory declaration on their statement of accounts from April 2020 until the termination or repudiation of the licence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The tenant will also be required to set out how he proposes to repay the outstanding rental arrears.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This will ensure transparency and accountability, but only in respect of tenants who terminate and have at least two months of the repayments instalments outstanding.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If any criminal behaviour is revealed – for example, if the tenant was using the period of relief to fraudulently dissipate assets – then there could be criminal sanctions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Tenants will also be expected to negotiate in good faith the terms of repayment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Any Court, when deciding whether the conduct is criminal, will likely take into account the totality of the conduct.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have also heard concerns from the REITs about potential constraints on their operating income and cashflow.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: REITs are concerned that they may be liable for additional tax and that their abilities to meet financial covenants in bank loan agreements could be affected.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They also worry that this could have a knock-on impact on S-REIT investors and the S-REIT industry as a whole.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We discussed this matter carefully with MOF, IRAS, MAS, the banks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: MOF and IRAS have temporarily extended timelines for the distribution of taxable income by S-REITs to qualify for tax transparency treatment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This will give S-REITs more flexibility to manage their cash flows and prevent them from incurring additional tax expenses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Corporate landlords, which include S-REITs, can also approach their banks or finance companies to explore funding if they face cashflow issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Banks have also assured MAS that there will be no automatic enforcement of loan covenant breaches for landlords impacted by the requirements under this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Besides cash-flow difficulties, what has been happening in the industry is that people face difficulties in a variety of other ways.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, take tenants whose tenancies expired or were expiring during circuit breaker period who had difficulties moving out because they were not allowed to go back to the office or shop to pack up or they could not find any movers or they are delayed because they cannot find workers to carry out the work, to put the place back to the original condition.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In such cases, it would be unfair for the tenant to have to pay double rent or similar charges under the contract or the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Bill allows us to deal with these situations, through subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will provide that a tenant who cannot vacate the premises due to COVID-19 may serve an NFR under the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the tenant will be protected from enforcement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In addition, the tenant will not be liable for double rent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In some situations, it might be fair for the tenant to pay some amount, especially if the tenant continued to derive benefit from the premises.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will prescribe the circumstances and how that amount can be assessed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These difficulties have also been caused to contracting parties, who may not themselves be parties to a construction or supply contract.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, a developer who has entered into a contract to fit out an office may be unable to do so within the timeline stipulated in the contract because of COVID-19 restrictions on construction work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That would expose the developer to liquidated damages for failure to deliver the fitted out office on time, through no fault of the developer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second example, say the tenant has entered into a tenancy agreement which provides for a three-month rent-free period for the purposes of renovation and fitting out, but is unable to proceed with construction works due to the COVID-19 restrictions, effectively losing the benefit of the rent-free period entirely.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The third example, a live example, a company, say Company A rents scaffolding materials from Company B, until 14 April for a project.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When the circuit breaker kicked in on 7 April, Company A could not return scaffolding materials because of the circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Company B says it is going to charge for an additional month of hiring fee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In these cases, the affected parties are not parties to the construction contract but they are parties to contracts that are nevertheless affected by the stoppage in construction work or other circuit breaker measures.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The precise scope of contracts, the obligations to be covered and the kinds of adjustments that Assessors may make will be set out with more clarity in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A similar approach will be taken for supply related contracts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: COVID 1 was passed and came into force in April this year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: During this period, we have observed that the operation of the Act has been effective.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The fact that out of the 4,000 Notifications, only slightly more than 10% have come forward, suggests that most of the others had managed to settle it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And because of the clarity of the previous Act, our understanding is that a lot of people have managed to deal with their issues along the lines provided for in the legislation without having to even file an NFR.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we have been talking to the Assessors to get feedback on how it is working.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, the information and matters disclosed in the course of proceedings before an Assessor, are to be kept confidential.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The cap will not apply to secured loan facilities given to SMEs, as well as hire purchase agreements taken out with banks and finance companies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: MAS has worked with banks and finance companies on various relief measures to support individuals and businesses affected by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These measures include principal repayment deferments for SME secured loans and hire purchase agreements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Borrowers can also extend their loan tenure to spread out their loan repayments over a longer period.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Banks and finance companies will also take into account their borrowers’ repayment ability after the relief period and adjust repayment plans if necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The reliefs contained in this Bill will have substantial impact.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are an estimated 31,000 SMEs in the F&B and retail sectors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They, their employees will benefit from the additional relief that is being granted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are moving this Bill to help our SMEs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We hope that businesses will be able to make good use of the easing of pressure to focus on transforming and levelling up to thrive in our new operating environment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And a large number of office and industrial tenants will also benefit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: While it is unusual, let me conclude by saying a little about the process for preparing this Bill, which runs into about 40 pages or so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At first sight it looks simple enough: two months plus two months.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Just to take one point: how do you pass down the waiver of rental relief through three or four layers of intermediate landlords?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What happens if one of them is a non SME?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When would the landlords give the reliefs and to whom?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And how do you handle the moratorium and the best balance between the different interests.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the aspects relating to smaller landlords, REITs, the types of tenants who should qualify.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And of course, the other contracts that should be dealt with in a myriad of situations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was a significant effort to conceptualise, crystallise, get the feedback from different stakeholders, take in the feedback and then, draft the legislation in about three weeks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I saw the best of the Public Service: how different agencies came together, worked round the clock.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: MTI and ESG gave us the data which allowed us to work out where the balance ought to be, who ought to qualify.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They attended all our meetings, including with stakeholders, helped to tweak our proposals and also worked their own loan schemes, and identified for us how the loan schemes may help.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: MAS played a crucial role in re-assuring the REITs as well as the landlords, and talking to the banks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They also attended all the meetings, including stakeholder meetings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I can say this – all roads lead to MOF and all roads lead from MOF as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They attended all our meetings, very supportive, facilitated and agreed to pay for the bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The private sector lawyers: Patrick Ang and Sushil Nair.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They did a lot of work here as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Committee members – I will put it as part of the record of my speech without having to mention all of them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Different stakeholders, if I can put a note down for the exceptional team in MinLaw, they put their heart and soul into this, led by the Permanent Secretary and Deputy Secretary, a team of highly motivated and talented young officers, worked round the clock.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And Justice Kannan Ramesh and his valuable expertise was very useful for us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Singapore is extremely fortunate to have him in Public Service.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Checking everything and making sure that it works, and again, working into the early morning hours, every day.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Attorney-Generals do not do that in most places.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I wish to thank them and put on record their contributions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They are responsible for the employment of more than 70% of our country's workforce, about two million workers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, during the circuit breaker, many have been left with empty offices or shops that rack up rent, incurring costs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This does not account for other operating costs, such as manpower costs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Reducing the costs that SMEs face will in turn help them support their workers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is good as it targets a significant expenditure many of our SMEs face and targets the period where SMEs are most adversely affected.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is fairer that landlords not have to take haircuts if their tenants' revenues had not been adversely affected.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Minister clarify what happens if the company was a new company or a new tenant such that the comparison to the previous year is either impossible or is an inaccurate comparison?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: From various news articles on this Bill, it looks to be that there is some distinction being drawn between large corporations and less large landlords through the use of the phrase "financial hardship".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is good as the considerations and ability to bear the "pain", so to speak, differs between smaller private landlords compared to large corporations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Just yesterday, Sir, 4 June 2020, I received an well-crafted email from a resident of Ulu Pandan.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And I quote from that email, and this is to support the point that I am making about the need to differentiate between different types of landlords.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In that email, my resident wrote, "Dear Mr de Souza, I hope this letter finds you well in these tough times.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am currently living on monthly rental revenue and honestly, I would not get to keep much of it after the banks take their due.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is my sincere wish that the Government would take into account of those in my position when discussing the proposed Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given the current economic situation, landlords in my position are already facing problems with rent collection as well as waivers and haircuts demanded by our tenants.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To further absorb an additional two months of rent would be too much for many to bear.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Of course, I begrudge not the tenants for their plight.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: COVID-19 is a natural and unexpected disaster that strikes at all levels of society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I just hope that they would try to understand that investing our savings into property should not entail a different treatment than those who invested in other forms of assets.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In times of crisis, we as a society must come together and help our neighbours as best we can.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I only hope that we would be allowed to contribute according to our means." I spoke with my resident this morning before coming to Parliament over the phone and I said I would definitely raise his well-worded point of view in Parliament this afternoon.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Drawing from my resident's message, the point I am making is this.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One, yes, I support the help given to tenants.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And I hope the Minister would be able to expand on this request of mine in the good Minister's reply.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It has been mentioned that direct monetary assistance previously rendered by the landlord to the tenant can be counted as part of the landlord's contribution to rental waiver.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Minister clarify whether agreeing to lower the rent, and not waiving rent, is also considered direct monetary assistance?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And if so, whether the rental waiver support from the Government and also the landlords' contribution to the rental waiver will be calculated based on rent pre-reduction or the newly agreed rent?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While the law has tried to strike a balance between the landlords and the tenants, it can only go so far in achieving an outcome that all parties will find mutually acceptable in the long-run.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Landlords and tenants need each other and I hope that they will continue to have constructive discussions to support each other through this unprecedented crisis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It was reported that landlords can apply for assessment as to whether the SME is eligible and that eligible tenants will be notified in due course.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It may be in the words of the draft Bill, but would the tenant also have access to the mechanism of assessing whether one, the landlord is indeed one that faces financial hardship or two, whether or not they are indeed an eligible tenant.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides rental waivers, the Bill also provides for rental repayment schemes to allow rent to be repaid in installments instead.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Minister clarify as to whether eligibility of this rental repayment scheme depends on whether the tenant had previously defaulted pre-COVID-19 or not?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Further, what will be done to ameliorate the knock-on effect such deferment has on private individual landlords who would face financial hardship owing to the lack of cashflow?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Will the Minister clarify as to how this will interact with rental waivers?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I should mention, Mr Speaker, that I am an advocate in private practice and I sometimes do have to delve in landlord-tenant disputes – just wanted to put that on the record.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The second main thrust of the Bill is that relating to contracts other than rents.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The last clarification I want to seek of the Minister is whether further adjustments will be made to the insolvency framework so that non-viable businesses can still exit smoothly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, where a business owner has made the hard decision to stop his trade in these times and seeks to venture into a new trade to overcome the difficult economic environment presented by the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And if it can reduce retrenchments; if it can help keep wages from being cut or further cut; if it strikes the right balance between tenant and landlord, if it gives that needed life buoy, as we come out of the circuit breaker and into the gradual reopening of the economy, then I say the effort is worth it, and the Bill should be supported.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Over the last two months, I have received many appeals for assistance from my residents who are SME business owners as they are facing cashflow problems.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The retail sector has been amongst the hardest hit as they have had to close their physical premises.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While some of them have been able to move their business online, overall business still has been impacted.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In the meantime, there are business costs and obligations still to be met and they still have to be paid.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For many SMEs, rent is a large part of the business cost making up about 25% to 30% of overall business cost.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Even as some businesses are able to start and reopen this week, they are not able to resume pre-COVID levels of operations immediately, and business demand will likely remain low.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Bill seeks to help SMEs ease some of the burden by ensuring that their accumulated rental obligations are shared among the Government and landlords.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The interventions in the Bill are quite substantive as it mandates that landlords will have to waive rent for SME tenants.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Bill also requires landlords to pass the Government granted tax rebates in cash grants as part of the Fortitude Budget to the SME tenants.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Bill does take a targeted approach and is reasonable.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It does not apply across the board to all SMEs and businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can Minister share if there has been an assessment of whether the rental relief measures will unnecessarily prolong the exit of unviable businesses, or benefit such businesses at the cost of landlords and taxpayers’ monies?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The rental reliefs do weigh in favour of tenants.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: At this point, I do want to declare my interest as I am a board member of a commercial REIT.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Minister did mention that other stakeholders, including landlords and REITs, have been consulted.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Minister has also shared that some of the views and concerns of these stakeholders who have been impacted are being addressed?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For example, the cashflow difficulties that have been expressed as well as the measures and mechanisms are being put in place to support these landlords.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While I am supportive of this amendment Bill, I am concerned that landlords may face financial hardship as a result of the additional rental waiver they have to provide to SME tenants.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For some of the smaller landlords, they may be dependent on the rental income to meet their own financial obligations.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Bill does state that for landlords who face difficulties in providing the additional waiver to SME tenants, it does provide some reprieve.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The landlords though will still have – if they are eligible for that reprieve – will still have to pay half of that obligation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And the landlords if they seek assessments on grounds of financial hardship, the assessments will take into consideration if the rental income forms a substantial part of their total income and the annual value of their properties.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Is that how it is going to be assessed?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And can Minister also share the assessment process and also how long that would take?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: SMEs play a crucial role in Singapore’s economy making up a majority of companies and do provide employment for more than two million Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So I do agree that SME tenants do need support during these tough times as they have been hard hit by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The rental reliefs will allow the SMEs the space to recover and in turn save jobs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We are dealing with survival of SME tenants that employ a substantial number of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We cannot afford to just depend on each individual landlord to determine what concessions should be granted to the tenants’ whose businesses are massively haemorrhaging.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such actions would be too slow and uneven and livelihoods will be at stake.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I must however acknowledge and commend the actions of a good number of landlords who took unilateral action to help the tenants.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For these landlords, I am glad to note that the amendment Bill is worded in a way that would take into account what these landlords unilaterally have done in assessing what further relief should be given by them to these tenants.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Whilst small businesses will be the immediate beneficiaries under the amendment Bill, in the long run, as hon Minister mentioned, this amendment Bill actually protects the landlord’s interest too because it will ensure that the tenant’s market will not collapse.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, just like COVID 1, this should not be seen as an anti-landlord bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Before moving on, I would like to applaud the consultation undertaken by the officers of MinLaw and all the other Government agencies that the hon Minister mentioned in coming up with this Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They worked, in the words of the hon Member Mr Christoper de Souza, "triple time" in taking consultation from the ground, identifying the big bug bear that SMEs have and providing concrete solutions through this Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Turning to the amendment Bill, I seek clarification on three areas and will end with a suggestion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, on the benefits that the sub-tenants will get under the amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As I recall, during the Second Reading of COVID 1, the hon Minister for National Development, Mr Lawrence Wong stated that tenants are not mandated to pass on property tax rebate to sub-tenants.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He explained that the reason for not mandating this is because, in his words, “there is a whole range of commercial arrangements” and there is no contractual relationship between the property owner and sub-tenant.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If the sub-tenants do not get the flow through of the benefit of the property tax rebate, based on my understanding, they will get a lower amount than the tenants in possession.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Will this also affect the rebate that these sub-tenants get from their landlord?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Because as I understand from the hon Minister's speech, the Government – for commercial tenants – will give two months' rental rebate and then the landlords will follow up with two months.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is a bit of a principle of reciprocity in action.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, will this affect what the sub-tenant will get?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, on clause 7 of the Amendment Bill, I note that it is proposed that a tenant who is holding over a property after the expiry of a tenancy owing to a COVID-19 event will not be liable to the landlord.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It makes eminent sense to provide such relief.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The control measures in place would make it difficult for the tenant to vacate premises, restore the property to its original state and yield vacant possession to the landlord.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such tenants may not be able to rely on COVID 1 if they entered into this lease after the trigger dates.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, if they enter into the lease after 25 of March 2020.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I note that in the amendment Bill, a Part 8 is proposed to provide relief to parties to downstream contracts affected by delay in performance or breach of a construction contract, supply contract or related contract.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It does not appear that Part 8 applies to leases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If my understanding is correct, may I please ask why leases, or for that matter, all the other scheduled contracts are excluded?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a matter of policy, I think it would have been better if parties in affected contracts that suffer a knock on effect arising from the application of the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) Act on scheduled contracts should also have recourse under this Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Third, I note that in addition to the rental relief, the Amendment Bill also provides for a statutory repayment schedule for accumulated rental arrears commencing from the month of November 2020 in equal installments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister refers to this as the third plank.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I further note that the landlords will not be able to charge contractual interest beyond the prescribed rate on the outstanding rent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This makes sense as it would otherwise whittle the effect of the rental reliefs that are being provided under this amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pillai asked for clarification on what a sub-tenant gets under the rental waiver and he pointed out that Minister Lawrence Wong had said during COVID 1 that the Bill did not mandate for the rebate to flow to the sub-tenant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In some cases, the businesses may be sub-tenants.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Minister Lawrence Wong, at that time, said, "the Government strongly urges and encourages all master tenants to pass on the savings from the rebate to their sub-tenants and to share the burdens during this time of uncertainty and difficulty." Minister Lawrence also explained that mandating further passing on of the rebates is difficult and complex because of the nature of the relationships that can arise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is why, in my opening speech, I said this is actually quite a complex issue.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we studied it and we decided that the complexity can be solved and can be dealt with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that is why, here we are mandating it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What we decided to do was not only enhance the Government assistance but also put in place a framework that ensures that the assistance reaches the intended beneficiaries who are the actual company or business that is using the premises for business.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What it does is put in place a framework of rental waivers mandated by law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Given this mechanism, the concern that is raised on behalf of subtenants not getting the two months of rental waiver does not arise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We did it very carefully and specifically because if you require the money to be passed down, then there can be all sorts of arguments as to who it would pass down to, when was it passed down and so on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But by law, we are saying that rental is not payable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Automatically, the subtenant does not have to pay his intermediate landlord, and the intermediate landlord does not have to pay the ultimate landlord.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What each of those in between might lose is that mark-up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the number of months of rental waiver a tenant will get does not depend on whether he is the tenant or sub-tenant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will set that out very clearly in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: IRAS will give a notification of cash grant to the owner of the premises because the owner of the premises has already received the money, everyone else does not have to pay rental.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about cases where an SME is a new company, which makes comparison to the previous year impossible or inaccurate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is another complexity which we did think about.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First of all, the reason why the same period of time was taken for a year-on-year comparison – it is a fairly normal thing and we did it to avoid seasonal fluctuations in revenue.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But where the tenants were not operational during the April to May 2019 period, we will choose another best appropriate period that will reflect whether the tenant's performance has been impacted by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For leases and licences that are even shorter, we will also work out the criteria.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked whether landlords who agreed to lower the rent will be able to set off the deduction against the rental waivers that they must provide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The rental waivers by landlords will be calculated based on base rent payable by the tenant for the applicable period.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or if they have already provided rental waiver, of course, they can take that into account.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The types of assistance from landlords that will be considered direct monetary assistance under the Act will also be prescribed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Jessica Tan asked about who the Assessors will be, the process for seeking assessment and the estimated timelines.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A panel of Assessors, professionals, a fair number of legal and accounting professionals – they have already been appointed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: More will be appointed to consider applications for assessments by landlords.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With regard to timelines, we will make the process as simple as we can.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have made it very simple under COVID 1.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The actual time taken for determinations to be made depends very much on the parties themselves and whether they adhere to the timelines.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, we will make them short and fast.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked whether tenants will have access to the assessment mechanism either to challenge the landlord's assertion of financial hardship or to ascertain whether they are eligible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The criteria for landlords facing financial hardship as well as the tenants' eligibility will be objective.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As for tenants, it will be IRAS which will make the assessment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the landlord wants to challenge that, he can.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the tenant wants to challenge the landlord's assertion of financial hardship, which will again be based on annual value of the property and what proportion of the rental income forms part of his total annual income, they will be allowed to challenge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pillai asked how we arrived at the 3% cap on interest in the repayment schedule and when it starts accruing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Interest at that cap rate will apply from the time that the rent was originally due and payable but the rent and interest will only be payable in accordance to the repayment schedule.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Interest at that cap rate will continue during the schedule repayment period until the arrears are paid off.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai referred to clause 7 on the relief for tenants who are unable to vacate their premises after the expiry of lease because of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He asked about whether there is a corollary provision to protect the landlords who have a back-to-back arrangement, with a new tenant to deliver vacant possession by a certain date.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is why I said this legislation is not simple, though it looks simple at first glance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are many related contracts that need to be thought through and we have provided for it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The landlord can serve a Notification for Relief on the new tenant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We imposed the rules that for those two months, there can be no work; and if there is a knock-on effect, that has got to be taken into account.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the landlord can tell the new tenant he cannot deliver vacant possession on time and the new tenant cannot terminate the lease on that ground.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This will give the landlord and the new tenant time to work out a compromise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If they cannot agree, they can apply to an Assessor who will make a determination to reach a just and equitable outcome.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about the interaction between this relief and the rental waivers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The rental waivers apply to the period during which the tenancy subsists.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Holding over or double rent is only relevant when the tenancy has already ended and is not subsisting.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali asked about whether leases are covered under Part 8.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Part 8 may apply to all contracts that may be affected by an upstream delay in construction, except those which may be prescribed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are looking at categories that should be excluded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, employment contracts should never be subject to these sorts of laws.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we also take the approach that only contracts which are actually written in, will be affected by the law as well and that will be gazetted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Jessica Tan asked if I could share how we have addressed the concerns of other affected stakeholders besides tenants and she mentioned that she is on the board of a REIT.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We consulted landlords, bigger landlords as well as smaller landlords, we consulted REITs, we consulted business people and of course, we had substantial assistance from MTI, ESG, MOF, MND, MAS, bankers and so on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, in the process of formulating these measures, we consulted all of them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We held engagements with all of them, got their views, we actually took substantive feedback and amended, adjusted our proposals where we thought that we ought to do so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You will see, as I have set out in the opening speech for the Second Reading, how we have come in to help the REITs, the landlords as well as the tenants, some by MinLaw, some by MAS talking to the banks, and some by IRAS and others, waiving some rules, amending them to help the REITs, for example.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Christopher de Souza mentioned that some distinction should be made between large corporate landlords, and smaller landlords who may themselves be facing financial hardship.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This will allow us to distinguish between larger landlords and those who are heavily dependent on rental income for their livelihoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The precise proportions, percentages will be set out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about the steps the Government is taking to ensure that those who are eligible for the rental reliefs are aware of this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would say, I think businesses who need relief would be very aware of this legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have had a fair bit of publicity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was in Deputy Prime Minister's Statement last week.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would be very surprised if anyone who qualifies is, at this point in time, not aware that they are going to get some benefits.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will put it out as much as we can.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And IRAS will notify property owners who have eligible tenants and the property owners will have to notify their tenants and sub-tenants as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Jessica Tan asked whether the rental relief measures would unnecessarily prolong the exit of unviable businesses, or benefit such businesses at the cost of landlords and taxpayers’ monies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is a very serious and important, fundamental question which more than troubled me and was front and centre in my consideration in deciding whether or not to intervene.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because we need to help but it cannot become a crutch and it cannot be such that unviable businesses, therefore, continue because we are using taxpayers' money.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the starting principle, I would say is this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we accept that COVID-19 was an exceptional event, then we ought to legislate for that as well in that whether it is viable or unviable, that is something that no one could have predicted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, the risk is not so much looking at unviable businesses but looking at viable businesses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the seas are still rough because Phase Two, it is not as if immediately, business is going to go back to normal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then Phase Three, how many people are going to go out?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How many people are going to spend money?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, business conditions are going to be tough.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it will only be the very fit, the viable businesses that will survive that period even with the relief that we are giving.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And none of us knows how long this will last.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But that is a larger piece of work.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Senior Minister of State, Mr Edwin Tong, second reading when?
